text: When a chat model writes a long answer, the first words usually arrive after a short pause, and then the rest stream out one token at a time. Behind that stream sits a structure called the KV cache, which trades memory for speed, and the size of that memory is one of the main reasons why context windows have limits at all.

Generation is a loop. The model reads the text so far, predicts one token, appends it, and runs again. Inside every attention layer, each position produces a query, a key and a value. The query says what this position is looking for, a key advertises what a position contains, and a value is what gets passed along when a query matches a key, rather like the index card in a library catalogue, which describes a book, sitting next to the book itself.

Because of the causal mask, the key and value at a position depend only on the tokens up to that position, so once they are computed they never change. A naive loop recomputes them for the entire sequence at every step, which is like rereading a novel from the first page every time you want to read one more sentence.

The KV cache simply keeps them. At each step the model computes the query, key and value for the single new token, appends the new key and value to the cache in every layer, and lets the new query attend over everything stored. The work per step shrinks from processing the whole sequence to processing one token, plus one row of attention scores against the cache.

This splits generation into two phases. In the prefill, the whole prompt is processed in parallel and the cache is filled, which is why the first token takes the longest. In the decode phase, tokens come one at a time, and each step must read the entire cache, along with all of the model's weights, from memory. That is why decoding speed is often limited by memory bandwidth rather than by arithmetic.

How big is the cache? For every token it stores one key and one value, in every layer and for every key-value head. So its size is two, times the layers, times the key-value heads, times the head dimension, times the bytes per number, times the tokens. For a model shaped like Llama 2 with seven billion parameters, in sixteen-bit precision, that comes to half a megabyte for every token, so a conversation of four thousand tokens holds about two gigabytes, for a single user.

Since the cache grows with the context length and with the number of users served at once, a great deal of engineering goes into shrinking it. Multi-query attention, proposed by Noam Shazeer in twenty nineteen, lets all the query heads share a single key and value head. Grouped-query attention, from Ainslie and colleagues, shares each key and value head among a group of query heads, and the largest Llama 2 model uses it with eight key-value heads. Serving systems such as vLLM store the cache in small fixed-size blocks, like the pages of memory in an operating system, so that very little of it is wasted.

So a context window is limited by more than the length a model was trained on: the cache grows with every token, and each new token must attend over all of it. With that picture in mind, the next lesson revisits a technique you have already used, retrieval-augmented generation, and asks what really happens inside the model when retrieved text is placed in its context.
